facts.fact_text: The first applicant is a legal entity registered under Georgian law on 8 November 2010.
The first applicant is a Georgian non-governmental organisation set up to promote and protect the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people in Georgia.
The first applicant planned to organise a peaceful march on 17 May 2012 in the centre of Tbilisi.
The peaceful march planned by the first applicant was intended to mark the International Day Against Homophobia.
On 8 May 2012, the first applicant gave the Tbilisi City Hall prior notice of its intention to hold a peaceful demonstration on 17 May 2012.
On 8 May 2012, the first applicant gave the Ministry of the Interior prior notice of its intention to hold a peaceful demonstration on 17 May 2012.
The first applicant informed the authorities of the planned route of the march, which would start from the grounds of the Tbilisi Concert Hall and proceed to Orbeliani Square.
The first applicant informed the authorities of the approximate number of participants in the planned march.

At around 1 p.m. on 17 May 2012, members of the LGBT community, staff members of Identoba and other LGBT activists, including the second to fourteenth applicants, gathered at the Tbilisi Concert Hall area, totalling approximately thirty people.
Shortly before the beginning of the demonstration on 17 May 2012, members of the Orthodox Parents' Union arrived in the Tbilisi Concert Hall area.
Shortly before the beginning of the demonstration on 17 May 2012, members of the Saint King Vakhtang Gorgasali's Brotherhood arrived in the Tbilisi Concert Hall area.
Approximately 200 metres from the starting point of the march on 17 May 2012, members of the Orthodox Parents' Union and the Saint King Vakhtang Gorgasali's Brotherhood confronted the LGBT marchers.
When the LGBT marchers reached Rustaveli Avenue on 17 May 2012, they were met by a hundred or more counter-demonstrators who were particularly aggressive and verbally offensive.
The counter-demonstrators blocked the LGBT marchers' way on Rustaveli Avenue by making a human chain and encircling the marchers, making it impossible for them to pass.
The LGBT marchers were subjected to threats of physical assault and to insults by the counter-demonstrators on Rustaveli Avenue on 17 May 2012.
The LGBT marchers, feeling threatened on 17 May 2012, immediately telephoned the police to alert them to the danger and request the immediate dispatch of additional police forces.
While waiting for additional police support on 17 May 2012, the LGBT marchers noticed a few police officers present at the scene on Rustaveli Avenue.

When the LGBT marchers approached the police officers present at the scene on 17 May 2012 and asked for help, the officers replied that they were not part of the police patrol and it was not their duty to intervene.
After approximately twenty to thirty minutes of escalating aggression on 17 May 2012, counter-demonstrators grabbed banners from the hands of several LGBT activists and tore them apart.
Counter-demonstrators resorted to physical attack by pushing and punching the LGBT marchers in the front row on 17 May 2012.
As a result of the counter-demonstrators' assault on 17 May 2012, the sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili), who was in the front line of the march, was knocked down, beaten and kicked.
The police responded to the third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze) by forcing him into a patrol car on 17 May 2012.
The police drove the third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze) to the Old Tbilisi Police Department of the Ministry of the Interior on 17 May 2012.
The third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze) was detained at the Old Tbilisi Police Department of the Ministry of the Interior for approximately twenty minutes on 17 May 2012.
The third applicant (Mr L. Berianidze) was given no official explanation for his arrest at the time of his detention on 17 May 2012.

The sixth applicant (Mr G. Demetrashvili), the seventh applicant (Ms G. Dzerkorashvili) and the tenth applicant (Ms M. Kalandadze), all employees of Identoba, were arrested by the police on 17 May 2012 when they moved from the pavement to the road.

On 27 March 2012, an amendment to Article 53 of the Criminal Code of Georgia was adopted pursuant to which discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity was recognised as a bias motive and an aggravating circumstance in the commission of a criminal offence.

Article 53 § 3(1) of the Criminal Code of Georgia provides that the commission of any offence listed in the Criminal Code on the grounds of any type of discrimination, including that linked to race, skin colour, language, sex, sexual orientation and gender identity, age, religion, political and other views, disabilities, citizenship, national, ethnic or social background, origin, economic status or societal position or place of residence, shall be an aggravating circumstance.

Pursuant to Article 161 of the Criminal Code of Georgia, illicit obstruction, perpetrated with recourse to violence, threat of violence or abuse of official capacity, of the exercise of the right to peaceful demonstration was a criminally punishable offence.

The International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA) noted in its 2013 Annual Review that the government of Georgia did not take measures to ensure effective implementation of the amended Article 53 of the Criminal Code, such as training the relevant police officers or taking actions to build confidence between law enforcement forces and the LGBT community.
